utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, Madam Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before we have the witness, are there any matters that the parties would like to bring to the attention of the Bench? Yes, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, in relation to this witness, I know that he has been called for the only purpose of cross-examination. And if you allow me, I would ask him just a few brief questions, perhaps 10 minutes, 15 minutes, so he gets warmed up for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you please state -- spell your name, Dr. Brunborg.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: My first name is Helge, H-e-l-g-e. And my family name is Brunborg, B-r-u-n-b-o-r-g.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I am a researcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in what field?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: In demography, or population studies it's also called.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who is your current employer?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Statistics Norway.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have a couple of exhibits which are a part of the Krstic record and we'll come to that. The first one is his CV, an updated version, and it's P727. I don't think we have to go into that. He can be cross-examined on that. I just have a few issues to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The first one, I understand, Dr. Brunborg, that you had -- you just came back from a recent assignment in the Middle East which is not mentioned in your CV. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I was asked by the UNFPA, United Nations Population Fund, to write a report on the effects of the separation barrier in the West Bank in the occupied Palestinian territory, on the effects of the -- on the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let me turn to your testimony in the Krstic case. I believe it was on the 1st of June, 2000. And this transcript has already been admitted by the Trial Chamber, and I believe you had a chance in my office to read through it. Do you have to make any comments on that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, I was reasonably satisfied with what I said then, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let me go back to your CV. I see there that you worked for the OTP, Office of the Prosecution -- Prosecutor for quite a while. Can you tell us in brief how come that you came to The Hague and worked for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: In 1996/1997, the Office of the Prosecutor felt the need for somebody to look at all the statistics that were floating around on the consequences of the conflict in Bosnia, especially the number of dead people, but also on refugees, displaced persons, and so on. They approached the Norwegian government, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and asked if somebody could be -- from Norway could be assigned to do this for a year. I was asked to apply, together with colleagues, and I was selected to do this. I came here at the end of June 1997 and stayed until the end of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us who -- with whom you dealt in -- while you were here in the OTP. What were the main persons you were tasked to work with?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning it was Morten Bergsmo, a lawyer, and John Ralston, who later became chief of investigations. And later many people in many -- many teams, including the team that worked on Srebrenica. I was assigned after a while to the leadership research team.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Brunborg. Now, you said that you worked on Srebrenica, and obviously that's why you came here today. Can you tell us who tasked you within the Srebrenica team in relation to Srebrenica-related projects.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, several people there, particularly Peter McCloskey and Jean Rene Ruez, who asked me to work on Srebrenica to validate and estimate the number of persons who went missing after the fall of the enclave of Srebrenica in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us a little bit more about the interactions you had with these people from the OTP. Did they tell you how to conduct your studies? Did they interfere with your standards, if you had any, in your specific field of work?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Not at all. My approach from the beginning, right from the time I came here, was to base my work on data on individuals, individual records as much as possible. Since it is much more difficult to lie or to cheat with individual records than with statistics produced by somebody else. So I immediately started to look at how can we collect lists of persons, of victims, during the conflict and of the population before the conflict and after the conflict, preferably in an electronic format so it was possible to do electronically process and compare and match this data. Fortunately there was a list -- I learned about a list of missing persons for Bosnia, and this was the starting point for the analysis of the missing persons from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, in your discussions with Jean Rene Ruez and Peter McCloskey, did you receive guidance in relation to whether you should be more liberal or more conservative or whatever in relation to your projects and indeed the numbers you were discussing?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: They told me to do very strict and to be very careful, very conservative. And they also told me that I should only include persons who were registered as missing after the 11th of July, 1995, and only persons whose place of missing was related to the fall of Srebrenica, that is near Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Thanks, Dr. Brunborg, I think we will come to that in a moment. Now, let me turn to the two reports which you drafted. The first one, the main report, is the report you had drafted for purposes of the Krstic trial dated 12th February, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that's Prosecution Exhibit 225 -- sorry, 725.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the second report which you had recently drafted, an addendum, dated 12th April, 2003, that's Prosecution Exhibit 726. Now again you had the chance to look at these reports in my office, and can you comment briefly about -- we'll go into details about the substance. But do you have general comments as to their accuracy as you see it?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I think they are -- still stand for everything I wrote here. Since then there may have been new data that came up. So that's the only thing I would have wanted to change, is to adjust for new data that has become available, but otherwise I'm reasonably happy with the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let's turn very briefly to the first report, the one which has been part already of the Krstic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the title, Your Honours, is, and I quote, "Report on the Number of Missing and Dead from Srebrenica." If the witness could be shown this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And perhaps while this is being done, if you could briefly tell the Trial Chamber the mandate that you were given, what was the purpose of the report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I was asked to estimate and validate the number of persons who went missing in connection with the fall of Srebrenica on 11 July, 1995. That was a brief mandate, but a lot of work to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you told us already one parameter you were given that -- one about dates and about time. I believe you said -- you were told only to include people from 11th of July onwards. Can you elaborate more about that. Was there also an end date to that window?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, the end date was the end of 1995, the 31st of December. But in practice there were very few missing persons -- very few persons who went missing after August of 1995, I think less than 100. So most of the missing persons went missing or reported as missing in July and August of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How about the territory of missing persons you were concerned [sic]?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: In that case, we were given a list of opstinas, that is, municipalities, and places in municipalities that were related to the fall of Srebrenica, which were not so far from Srebrenica in itself. And only those places were included among the missing. People who were reported as being missing from other parts of Bosnia were not included.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us - and perhaps you could use Prosecution Exhibit 731 - can you tell us the main finding of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I think it could be helpful if it could be placed onto the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And perhaps you can start with the last figure before you explain how this figure is reached.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The bottom line is 7.475 Srebrenica-related victims. That is missing and dead persons. And we see that I have arrived at this figure through adding and subtracting the numbers above. There were -- we used several lists of missing persons, in fact two lists from the ICRC, that is a national Red Cross committee, and two lists from PHR, that is physicians for human rights. We found that 5.712 victims were on both lists after we had merged them. And 1.586 on the ICRC lists only. And 192 on the PHR list reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So after combining these two lists from these two different sources, ICRC and PHR, you came to a number of 7.490?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us the methods ICRC and PHR used to collect these names?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The ICRC and PHR are both non-governmental organisations with different mandates. One of the mandates of ICRC is to trace persons who go missing in a conflict to unite family members. If there is a chaotic situation, people lose track of each other. So they -- throughout the conflict in the former Yugoslavia, starting in 1991, I believe, they had offices that registered people as missing. When somebody was missing, the relatives, they could go there and give them the particulars about the person. And I believe they have channels and ways of searching for people all over the former Yugoslavia and in the rest of the world, in fact. Whereas PHR, they had a different mandate. They started their work in 1996, and the major purpose was to help in identifying people who would be exhumed from mass graves or from graves related to the fall of Srebrenica. So they would ask their relatives who came forward for different kinds of information, like special physical characteristics, special clothing, and so on, to help in the identification. This also assisted later DNA analysis of the body parts that were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I see that if we go back to your exhibit, that you have compared this intermediate result of 7.490 to the voters registers of 1997 and 1998. And we see that you deducted the number of 9. Can you explain this process.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, people who are missing and believed to be dead should not be able to vote. So when we had this complete list of people who were registered to vote in 1997 and 1998, we wanted to make a comparison to see if there were, in fact, people believed to be missing who were registered to vote. So we did a very careful comparison, and we found nine names that we believe are unique and that are appearing on both lists of missing persons and the list of voters. So there is an error somewhere. Either these are not really missing persons, they are survivors, or somebody misused their identities because they knew they were dead, so they misused their identities, perhaps to get extra -- additional political influence, to vote twice. Or third, there is a mix-up due to data problems and so on. But the conclusion is that the number was very small. Nine, that is less than -- that is about one-tenth of a per cent. To be on the safe side, we subtracted these names, although it is not certain that these are survivors.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Then turning back to your chart you have deducted another six persons from the list of missing in Srebrenica 1995. Can you tell us why you did that.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: We asked the ICRC whether they knew about people who had survived, who they later learned to be survivors and not dead on the list of missing persons since January 1997. And they told us there were six persons out of 7.000, but they would not reveal their identities to us. So to be on the safe side, we subtracted another six persons from the total number. We could not delete those from the list that was also submitted to the court, because we didn't know their identities. In this way we ended up with 7.475. By the way, some or all of these six people may be included in the nine people who are above, but again to be on the safe side, we excluded them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, to sum up these calculations, how reliable do you think this number of 7.475 missing persons is it?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: We think that the number is very reliable as a minimum estimate. There cannot be many cases, if any, that are wrong amongst these. On the other hand, the number could easily be higher because there were records that we excluded to be on the safe side, not only these 15 but other records also where there was inconclusive evidence. There could also be missing persons who were not registered by the families or other people. So probably there may be a few more hundred. But we did not know at that time. So it's very reliable on the lower side but not on the upper side you could say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Brunborg, I see that the title of this chart says, "Srebrenica-related Missing and Dead Persons." Now, are these missing persons coming from these two lists, ICRC and PHR, are these people dead? Do you have an opinion about that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, most likely all or most of them are dead. First, in one of the ICRC lists, 600 persons were listed as being declared dead. So on the ICRC list, 600 are already declared dead. Then there are a number of other indications showing that these people -- most people or all are likely to be dead. If I may mention briefly the major argument is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you perhaps can mention on which page.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: On page 10 there are -- in my 2000 report, there are four arguments. Indications of why these are dead. In 2000, there are only 1900 bodies had been exhumed, but only 70 had been identified. And of these 70, 66 appear on our list of missing. Then -- so those are dead, of course, those 66. Then the age distribution of Srebrenica-related missing persons and exhumed bodies is very similar, which can be shown in another -- which is shown in another exhibit. You may give them the number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you -- I guess if you talk about Exhibit Number 735.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct. Thirdly -- or perhaps fourthly, since the ICRC started registering Srebrenica-related victims in July of 1995, only 22 persons had been found alive or those registered as missing. And finally, as I mentioned, only nine Srebrenica-related missing persons who were found on the voters lists from 1997 and 1998. So these are all indications that point in one direction, that they are dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, to finish up this brief introduction, I believe you have published the findings of your report. Indeed it's been available in public. And I think you also drafted a few publications yourself based on this Krstic report. Can you tell us how the academic community and the practitioners in your field of science specialisation has received your report?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object. Now he's going to be vouching for the credibility of the articles that he wrote based on what members of his association or his scientific community thinks of it. I don't think it's proper. If they want to introduce somebody from the academy of sciences who says, we've read his report, we've read his methodology, and we give it the seal of approval. That's fine. But for the gentleman to comment on how his brethren are commenting about his own articles, I think it's a little bit too much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Waespi, maybe you could be more specific concerning those comments or whether there have been a paper in a certain kind of forum or whether it has been quoted or relied upon, but just the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you give any presentations to your colleagues and other interested persons?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: On several occasions. Population Association of America, a large conference on the statistics development and human rights in Montreux in Switzerland in 2000. The conflict research seminar in Uppsala in Sweden. And several other international national and national meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how was it received?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: With great interest and very well I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us, this study you are presenting, compared with statistics, as you have been doing it before you came to the Tribunal, is that something new which you have developed?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Not really, because in -- I live in a country where we had very good data on individuals in Norway. We have a personal identification number and a central population registry since 1964. And we're very used to matching data from different sources. So we have a population register and from another registry we have income, from a third registry we have education, and we can merge all these data sources together to find out about the relationship between education and income, for example. So that approach was not new. The difference for Bosnia was that the data were quite faulty. There is a unique identification number called "maticni broj," but it has often errors, and it is not used in all sources. But the basic approach was the same. But we had to do much more data cleaning and data evaluation than is -- than I have to do in Norway.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And my last question is: Can you tell the Trial Chamber how this area is called, you know, the assessment of numbers of victims of an area in an armed conflict? Do you have a name for that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, this is in a way an emerging new area that is now called the demography of conflict and violence, which I also have contributed to establishing. There is a working group in the International Union of the Scientific Study for Population chaired by me on this topic. There was a large seminar in Norway in November. And several journals will publish special issues on papers related to the demography of conflict and violence, which has both to do, dealing with the consequences of conflict, that is, number of deaths, number of refugees, effects on births, and so on, but also on demographic causes of conflict, say high population growth, high population pressure, youth bulges, do they increase the likelihood that there is violent conflict effect. So this is an emerging field that is achieving a lot of interest, getting a lot of interest, both from demographers and from conflict researchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Waespi. Cross-examination, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, if I could have just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Brunborg.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First, let me just get to your CV so we can get that out of the way. As I understand, you just came back from the Middle East. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, from the sounds of the project, you have been tasked to figure out what effects the barrier that the Israeli government is putting -- to separate itself from the Palestinians. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now the effects, are we talking about economic effects?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, social effects. Effects on migration, housal [sic] composition, social relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, is that in the field of demography or is that in the field of sociology or is it a combined field?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, migration and housal composition is in the field of demography. This other social relations is more in the field of sociology, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, from looking at your CV it appears to me that you specialised in economic demography?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would that be the field where you're trying to figure out incomes, how labour -- how the labour force works, migration of labour, those sorts of things?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. But I would also like to say that since I finished my Ph.D., most of my work has been related to more pure demography and not so much to economic demography, which my CV will show.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I wasn't getting to your CV. I was merely asking what you got your Ph.D. in, okay? Now, as I understand it from listening to you, you were, in essence, seconded from the Norwegian government to the Office of the Prosecution. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct. Until -- I believe it was at the end of 1997 this [indiscernible] institute was abolished because of opposition in the -- at the United Nations, so then I was transferred to a regular UN contract.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I want to get to that in a little bit. You indicated that from June 1997 until the end of the year, that would have been six months, you were assigned by your government to assist. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So it was after that six-month period that you began to work as a contract employee for the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I think the dates are correct, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, how long did you work as a contract employee with the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Until the end of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So we're talking about approximately a total of year and a half working with the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, while you were -- for the year of 1998, were you back in Norway teaching or doing other projects, or were you exclusively dedicating yourself to this project?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It was full-time, but I took some vacation days off to do some teaching in Norway. I had some shorter teaching assignments that I wanted to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I can understand that. Now, the UN is pretty generous, at least from a private sector's point of view, with respect to vacation time. I think it's six weeks a year, perhaps even longer, when you count in all the UN holidays. Was that above the six-week period?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So within that range?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Were you also -- maybe I should slow down a little bit because of the translation, you know, and I'm a little nervous, you know. I don't know why, but I am.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, I think I have more reason to be nervous than you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, maybe we can work our way through this process. In any event, while you were working for the Office of the Prosecution, were you out in the field as well or were you basically here?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I made four trips to Bosnia, during that period 1997/1998, and one trip in 1999 when I was more of a consultant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during those trips, was that for the purpose of getting yourself oriented to the landscape, or was it for you to actually go into archives, meet with various offices to see what data you might be able to collect? What was the real purpose of that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: To collect data, to find out what data were available and to request that data.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and the witness please make pauses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us where exactly did you look for data?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I first went to the statistical office in Sarajevo. And I went to the OSCE, that is the organisation for security and cooperation in Europe. And to various governmental and non-governmental organisations, mostly in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I would suspect by that time and for sure by this time you know that in Bosnia you have the federation -- the entity of the federation and another entity called the Republika Srpska. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, and I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And of course Sarajevo is the capital for Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that's where the state offices are. Right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I -- incidentally, do you know in which of the two entities Srebrenica is located?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Certainly, in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever make any efforts to contact or search -- well, let's say start with contacting officials in the Republika Srpska to see whether you could collect any data from them?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In fact, I had planned -- I was planning a trip to Banja Luka in December 1999. And I remember the day. It was heavy snow fall. I was going to drive in a Land Rover to Banja Luka in the afternoon. I was not looking forward to it. Then I was told at 2.00 that you cannot go, because there has been an arrest of General Krstic. So the security situation is too difficult. So I never made it to Banja Luka. But I have talked to people from Republika Srpska later. And also after my first visit, there was established an overall statistical agency for all of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There's one federation office in Sarajevo, one for Republika Srpska in Banja Luka. And there is an agency for statistics I think it is believed [sic]. And headed by a three-person body, one Muslim, one Croat, and one Serb, and I met those on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But suffice it to say - and I'm just trying to be rather direct on this - you never physically went to Banja Luka to, say, visit the bureau of statistics of the RS?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I tried but I did not get the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand you've tried. But there's been a whole lot of time between the Krstic arrest and his trial, in fact. So the answer is you did not go?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct. But on my behalf the Office of the Prosecutor made several written requests to the Office of the Prosecution for data.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, was that -- were those requests made to specific agencies or collection offices, such as the Bureau of Statistics?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: They went through the government, through the special liaison officer based in The Hague. And I think they went to different, like, Ministry of the Interior, Bureau of Statistics, and different agencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question. I'm trying to give the interpreters a break. I'm sure they're going to appreciate that. Did you -- when you began working, did you at any point in time make a comprehensive list of all the official agencies or offices, be they in Serbia, Croatia, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or the Republika Srpska, did you make a list of all those sorts of places that might have relevant data to your project?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I think I can say yes, but it -- the list was not a fixed one. As I learned more about institutions, I investigated, approached, either in person or through correspondence, sometimes through telephone, whether they had data that was available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I've been to Norway; lovely country, runs like a Swiss clock. And as you said, you can get all sorts of data. And I take it that if somebody were to go to Norway, they would ask somebody like yourself where they could collect data. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you, not being from the Balkans, you know, this region, and specifically not being from Bosnia and Herzegovina, did you ever contact anyone from the region or the former Yugoslavia to get a handle on the various agencies or organisations, official organisations, that collect data?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, I talked to many people about that. I asked everybody I met almost: Do you know about organisations, institutions, NGOs, government agencies that have data? So that permitted all my work to do that [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But you would agree with me that asking, for instance, Peter McCloskey, who is from the United States, or Mr. Ruez, who is from France, is not going to be terribly helpful? I mean, they may have some knowledge but they're not going to know the nitty-gritty, all the little places that you might find statistics. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Asking NGOs that are international might be of assistance, of course. But my question is: What about domestic, people from the RS, for instance, or people from the Federation, or people from the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did you actually contact somebody in particular who would be able to tell you this organisation collects data with respect to movement or households or number of births or what have you?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. And my first approach was, of course, the statistical agency in Sarajevo, which because I used to work in a statistical office myself and they have the mandate to collect and disseminate all statistics for a country. And that was the same for Bosnia, so that was my first approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So that was the state office?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: But I also talked to, as I said, a number of other individuals and institutions, including, say, the office of the high representative, and embassies and so on, because I was not familiar with that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, the office of the high representative is primarily composed of foreigners working there, all right, so they are hardly in a position of being experts as far as how the RS government keeps statistics. Wouldn't you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, but they knew about data collected by foreign organisations like the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What if I were to tell you that at the time that you went to Sarajevo, that it's my understanding that they were not collecting data relevant to the RS, such as the data that we just discussed. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At the time that you went to Sarajevo, it's my understanding that the Sarajevo -- the state office was not getting all of that data from the RS, because as you well know, there's been some -- there's some ongoing friction, although much less today than in the past?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I was fully aware of that, yes. And I heard rumours about some friction between those -- between the two entities, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we get -- launch into your reports and your articles, I must confess that I was rather taken aback yesterday evening at 6.00 or slightly thereafter when I was informed by Mr. Waespi that there is this ongoing effort by the demographic team at OTP, that they have generated a report or a draft, and that apparently you are involved in or consulting with that particular team with respect to this project.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. My question is: Was this news to the Office of the Prosecution yesterday at 6.00 in the afternoon, or had they known about this information before?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think that's a question for the Prosecution to ask. I'm not sure whether Mr. Brunborg can answer when the Office of the Prosecutor was involved or informed about an ongoing project.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect, this gentleman has been working in the Middle East. Obviously they had to make contact with this gentleman, the demographer's work for the Office of the Prosecution, obviously it would seem at least logical that members working for the Office of the Prosecution would know that there is this ongoing study and that Mr. Brunborg, because of his association with OTP, his expertise, you know, the institutional knowledge on the project would also be involved. And I guess it's a way -- I'm trying to figure out: Is he aware, in his conversations with Mr. McCloskey or Mr. Waespi or somebody else on this team, whether he had told them that there is this ongoing project. Because, as I said, I learned of this for the first time 6.00 yesterday evening. We've had a fairly long weekend, and I just think that it's rather coincidental that I get it right before I'm supposed to do my cross-examination. And I just want to know whether this gentleman knows anything about that. And if he doesn't, that's fine. I'll accept it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I believe that you have to rephrase your question in a certain way, because your question is truly posted to the Prosecution rather than the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll rephrase, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Brunborg, did you inform the Prosecutor that you had been working or assisting in this ongoing project? Had you informed them prior to yesterday afternoon, say 6.15 when I got the call in the middle of watching the news?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you tell me -- do you know about what date, what time frame, it might have been that you had informed them that there was this ongoing process and that you have been involved with and that there was a draft report being prepared?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I think I learned about that soon before Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it you communicated this to the Prosecution, that there was this draft report coming out?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, the draft report was written by the Prosecution, the OTP, so I did not need to inform them about their own work, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it sounds pretty logical to me. So I think we solved that conundrum. Well, I'm going to reserve any questions with regard to this because I haven't had a chance to study it. Let me just focus now on some of your other work. And incidentally the report that we're talking about is basically an update of what you had built on. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's not something entirely new?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I would suspect that the same methodology that you applied is currently being applied by the folks in OTP?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct. May I say why I think it is important that this work continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I never said that it was unimportant, now, did I?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No. But may I say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, you don't have to say it at this point in time. Because I will -- well, I will agree with you that it's very important, but that's not the purpose why we're here. If you can agree with me that I have been sandbagged a little bit, and sideswiped a little bit, you know, I think that's more important at this stage, but I agree that it's very relevant Now, before we get into your reports, let me be upfront with you with respect to where we stand as a Defence. In other words, I'll give you a preview of our case. First, we have never contested, nor do we contest, that atrocities occurred during the fall of Srebrenica or thereafter; nor do we contest that a large number of people, the number of which is unknown but in the thousands, were executed, okay. We know that there is a large number of people missing. So I think that we're not that far apart as far as what occurred and maybe even somewhat in the same vicinity as to how many people are missing. All right. So that's not going to be much of an issue, though I do want to talk to you about your methodology, and I have some more pointed questions with respect to our particular case. Okay. Now, if we could just start with: Could you please tell us, if you know, if you're able to, what was the number of people that had left through the exodus, as you put it in your report or one of your articles, through the woods to make it to Tuzla? What was the number of people that were killed as a result of non-executions?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you tell us why you do not know?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Because the cause of death is not given for the people I estimated the number. The only source I have is which is mentioned in my addendum is the NIOD report, the Dutch -- the war -- what do you call it, the war institute. And they said that by quoting two Serb sources, 1500 men were taken as prisoners of war, subtracting those from the 7.500, approximately, that leaves 6.000 that could be -- that were killed. That is their conclusion. But they also say that it can never be known with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I didn't want to get ahead of myself, but since you've already got us there, let's just discuss that. In one of your reports you do, among other things, go through the report that was prepared by the RS that was in answer to basically the OTP's, or the results that were -- that are published with respect to how many people perished or disappeared or are missing as a result of the fall of Srebrenica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, no, not quite I'm afraid. I learned that the RS report was actually first written in 1998, I did not learn this until yesterday, and translated and published in 2000. So they did not have a chance to consider my report or the OTP report, so their criticism is a critique of the ICRC list of missing persons, not our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In any event -- and thank you for clarifying that. In your addendum, which is for identification purposes P726 of 12 April 2003, you do an analysis of this particular report. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. I look at some of the arguments raised in the report as if they were against our list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Okay. And one of the things that you wanted to do was pre-empt, I would suspect, or answer or counter any arguments that may have been made or could be made by the RS against your report. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. I think it would be more open, more honest, to present the arguments in writing instead of as a surprise in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Fair enough. And of course at no time have we ever accepted this report of having any credibility or validity, so we get that straight. Now, if we go to your mentioning of the NIOD report, which is found on -- I always seem to have an unnumbered article. It's on paragraph 5, number 5.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's right above the conclusion. But there you do mention the NIOD report. And there you state that the VRS estimate -- that of the 7.500 persons that are missing, they came up with 1500, approximately, dying on their way to Tuzla as a result of or based on the VRS estimate of 6.000 prisoners of war. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, with the RS report, you allot yourself two -- a little bit over two full pages of a response. And I notice here that you don't respond one way or the other with respect to the NIOD report. Was there a particular reason?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, the RS report I found interesting, because not only as, say, part of the -- witness for the Prosecution, but also intellectually, other data that could contradict in any way my findings. Because I always have doubts whether, is this really correct, is there something I overlooked. So I was very interested in seeing that. That's why there is a lengthy discussion. Now, the NIOD report doesn't address this issue very much at all. So that's why there is just a short paragraph, but I wanted to make aware of this issue of -- the conclusion on approximately 1500 people killed, which is a very uncertain estimate because it's very rough. But I would also like to say that I was not asked to find out how many -- how people were killed or who did it, just the number of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that. But there may be a purpose why I'm asking these questions which at this point in time may not seem obvious or relevant. Upon looking at the NIOD report, did you by any chance contact anybody that was preparing the report to find out who at the VRS estimated that there was 6.000 prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And from your analysis based on -- and with the qualifications that you have stated, as you sit here today you cannot tell us with any degree of certainty of the some 15.000 people that were reported to have left through the woods to Tuzla, how many exactly perished or disappeared or went missing as a result of military activities on their way?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And so we don't know whether that 1500 is on the high end or the low end or the average -- or the acceptable range. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: And it's about the only estimate I've seen also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I take it, given your answers, if I were to ask you -- I think I know the answer but we want it for the record. If I were to ask you: Of those people that perished, how many of them were actually from Srebrenica and not refugees from other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina or Eastern Bosnia, could you give us that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, after the 2000 report and the presentation of it in the Krstic trial, we matched the missing persons with this census 1991. And we could then assess the residence of the missing persons in 1991, where they lived. And we found out that of those 7.500, approximately 56 per cent were enumerated in Srebrenica in 1991. So a little more than half of them lived in Srebrenica. Most of the others lived in Bratunac and Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I don't want to get into that area yet. But let's say just for the moment that we accept that figure, okay. I'm not saying that I'm not accepting it, but let's just for the sake of argument at this point in time we accept that figure. Would you be able - since we don't know, since we don't know how many people perished on their way in the woods - you cannot tell us with any degree of certainty what the percentage of those people might have been?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, but it is probably -- approximately the same proportion of it, I would say. If I may, in the -- when people register people as missing, they said place of disappearance, and quite a few noted forests or mountain. And probably thinking of the track through the woods. But I don't recall now the number. We could find out the number of people who were reported as being missing in the forest or mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you never did the calculation?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: We looked at it at one time, but I don't recall what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But if we look at your charts, we could not at this point in time -- I'm not saying it's impossible to create, but at this point in time if we look at your chart, we cannot find a breakdown of how many people would have been missing in the woods versus those who are missing elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And of course you weren't asked to do that, I take it?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But as I understand it, your initial mandate called for you to simply find out how many people went missing as a result of the fall of Srebrenica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I also understand from reading your addendum -- I think it's in the addendum. You kept me busy this weekend, I must say. It's in one of your reports. That the other issue was how many of them were from the Srebrenica area. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So there were two main tasks: How many missing and how many of those missing were from the Srebrenica area. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I take it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, are we going until 3.30?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm about to launch into an area which I hate to break. I don't mind, but if we could have an earlier break so then I could -- because I don't want to get into it, and the gentleman may be confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe we could have our break now. We'll resume at five minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Brunborg, just a last couple of questions I forgot to ask regarding the NIOD report. You did point out, or they stated in their report: "It remains impossible to state with any certainty how many men were executed following the fall of Srebrenica and how many perished during the march to Tuzla. It is likely that we shall never know." Now, do you agree or disagree with that part of the NIOD report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, I agree in principle. I think it may be possible to get a little bit closer, though, as exhumations are progressing and if people are found blindfolded in mass graves and so on, I think that is a clear indication of execution. But that work is in progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- and would it be fair to say that identifying those who were executed is probably a slightly easier - especially under those conditions - than, say, those who might have died of gunshot wounds on their way to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. And there are also many of those who died on the way to Tuzla may not be buried in -- many of them are probably not buried in any grave at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And I understand you're not a pathologist, but I thought I would ask for your opinion nonetheless. So anyway, Mr. Brunborg, in your conclusions, if you look at the very last one, that's on paragraph 6. Again I'm referring to Prosecution Exhibit 726. Now, you state here on the very last one: "Similarly, claims that the missing persons did not die in connection with the fall of Srebrenica but later in other armed confrontations are not convincing, as the presented evidence is inconclusive and covers only a relatively small number of persons." My question is: Are you referring to those who might have died during the trek towards Tuzla over here? Is this -- in other words, when I read this, I had the feeling that perhaps you were presenting a counter-argument to the portion of the NIOD report that we just discussed.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, not really. I was thinking more of the arguments claimed in the Banja Luka report that some of the persons claimed to be missing were transferred from Srebrenica soon after the enclave alive and went to Zepa and other places and died in battles there. And so they were not missing from Srebrenica, the fall, but from some other conflict. That's what I was referring to. And perhaps there are some cases like that, but not a very large number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You are aware, of course, that of the reported 15.000 number of individuals that left towards Tuzla, it's reported - we don't have exact data - that about one-third, that would make it about 5.000 of them, were actually armed soldiers. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I've heard about that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And of course we don't have some kind of a statistical breakdown as to the age bracket for the people that left towards Tuzla. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Unlike, for instance, for the separation where we have pretty good information in evidence that those who were separated were generally between the ages of 16 and 60, which was the military age. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct. But of the total number of missing persons, most of them are also in that age bracket, including -- which includes people who trekked through the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. Which would all make them combatants or potential combatants?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Potential, not necessarily combatants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Not necessarily. And if we were to take -- again, just to make sure that I got it right. If we were to accept your figure of 7.000-plus, you cannot tell us whether a third, a half, or more of that numerical figure that you've come up with actually perished in the woods or perished as a result of the executions?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, I cannot. But we could look at the place of disappearance, and include, say, how many were listed as disappearing in the forest or mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, many of them were claimed to have disappeared in Srebrenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, as you know - or maybe you don't know - but the individuals that left towards the woods had gathered, as I understand the evidence, sometime around the 10th of July. And then around the early morning of the 11th, as I understand it, they began to make their trek. My question is: Do you know -- do you have an exact figure as to how many people were actually killed in Srebrenica during the period of the conflict there, that is between the 6th of July and the 11th of July, when Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, I do not. I have read reports about the fighting and what happened then, but I don't recall any numbers of killed persons in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you don't exclude the possibility, though, that some of the people that went missing from Srebrenica could have been -- and I would suspect the number is small, but nonetheless could have actually been killed during that period of the conflict leading up to the fall of Srebrenica, that is between the 6th of July and the 11th of July. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is possible. But if they were listed as missing, registered missing by relatives, and they were last seen on the date before the 11th, they have not been included in our list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But those are some pretty big ifs. Right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. But if they were witnesses to many of these -- to the fighting, and I'm sure that many of those that were killed then were seen by witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we're going to get into that. But just since you raised the issue, did you by any chance check any data, just do a random sampling, to see whether those incidents were reported, to see whether verifiable information was presented by family members that would give you some sort of confidence that that data was actually collected and of course was reliable and verifiable?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Not really. We relied on checking the -- comparing data with other data sources. I did meet with families and victims' families, though, to get an impression on -- especially the situation when the registered -- the families -- their relatives as missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we know that some fighting occurred and we know that a certain number -- we don't know the exact, but we know that there were fatalities on both sides. Do you know whether there were any registrations of people missing between the period of 6 and 11 from the Muslim community of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but the Bosnian army, the Federation army, they registered all their killed soldiers, and they have data lists, lists of people who were killed in action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And naturally you checked that data for the month -- for the days of the 6th of July and the 11th of July to make sure that you excluded any potential - how should I put it - mistakes?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, that list was not available when I did this work, but it has later been acquired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you say it wasn't available, was that because the Federation army refused to turn it over to the Office of the Prosecution or was it unavailable because perhaps you were unaware of that list being in existence?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: First I did not know that there was such a list, but I was in contact with some sources in Bosnia, also military, and there was -- I sensed a great reluctance at that time to hand over anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, sensing a reluctance is like the way I feel when I come to court, my gut really is turning upside down, you know, that's a gut feeling, as we call it. So -- and given that you are a scientist, could you tell me whether indeed you made a specific request for that, as opposed to sensing a reluctance, hence being reluctant to ask for it?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I don't recall. I think I asked for the OTP to make a request through the liaison office on military deaths.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand it - and I might be wrong, I don't know - but rumour has it that AID, the secret service, basically, of the Federation has been working hand in glove with the Office of the Prosecution since almost the inception of the Tribunal and actually working here. Now, do you know whether any requests were made through AID to get that information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I not sure whether that comment is really helpful for the witness to answer the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If he is aware of it, Your Honour. He is aware that AID, the secret service, was working, and as I understand it, Your Honour, and I can be corrected by my colleague here, that AID has gone through great lengths to assist the Office of the Prosecution in providing them with relevant documents to their cases. We're talking about Srebrenica. Obviously the Federation army has no reasons to withhold evidence that would provide some insight and guidance as to how many of their soldiers might have perished during that fight. So I'm merely asking the question. The gentleman can tell me he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, your question: "Do you know whether any requests were made through AID to get any information," is perfectly okay. The other words I don't think is necessarily. Just ask your question directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Your Honour. Sometimes it is helpful to sort of comment a little bit to let the witness know that I do know, as opposed to getting a no and then I'm stuck with the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But in any event, sir, do you know whether AID was asked to provide any such information?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I do not recall. I would need to ask OTP to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Naturally at some point, having become aware of such a list, surely you must have insisted on those records in order to have a most accurate - if that is possible - but a most accurate accounting. Would I be correct in assuming that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, I was very interested in an accurate accounting. But may I also repeat that I was not asked to consider the cause of death and/or military or civilian deaths. So I was not really very much concerned about that. But for the total picture, for the total number of deaths related to Srebrenica and for all of Bosnia, I would like to include military deaths as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well -- I'm waiting for the translation. Well, given your mandate, as I understand it, it was the Office of the Prosecution that picked those magic dates, that is, July 11th to end of August -- or I think it was 31, August 31 --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, actually end of December 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: End of December. But in reading your report it seemed that initially it was until the end of August, and then that mandate grew until the end of December. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So we know that Srebrenica fell on the 11th. We know that most of the atrocities occurred within a four- to five,- six-day period. And I say most. We do know that some people were still trying to make it to Tuzla. What was the justification given to you by the Office of the Prosecution that you should try to locate missing people that were reported all the way up until December 1995, or the end of December 1995?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Because there might be some relatives who did not report their relatives as missing before, and they were not sure when they were seen last alive and so on. But in any case, it wasn't a very large number after 31st of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What was that number?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I believe it was less than 100. It's written in my report; I could find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so, given that they told you these were the dates, you didn't think it was necessary to try to find out how many people might have been killed from the 6th to the 11th?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, I understood it that it was exactly to eliminate such cases, that the starting date should be 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, let's switch the topic a little bit, and I want to talk about your project. In reading your reports and your articles and your testimony, one walks away with the -- a conclusion that there was a lot of unknown data not available to you at the time that these reports were made. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact, that data continues to remain unavailable or unknown to us. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Partly correct only. Some of the data has later been collected by my successor Ewa Tabeau and her colleagues, say, list some military deaths and data both from Republika Srpska and from the Federation, data on exhumed bodies, more missing persons and more dead persons. So a lot of data had been collected after I finished this project, including regular data on the deaths from the federal statistical office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It appears now from your answer that there was a list of military deaths. Did you look at that list prior to making your --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I did not get that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, do you know when it was received?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No. Well, I think it was received in 2001 or 2002. It has been later used by Ewa Tabeau to -- for further work, which was included in the documents that you received last night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's wonderful --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Or mentioned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But nonetheless, from listening to you, it would have been available to you prior to your preparation of your addendum to your initial report that you made back in 2002?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Possibly, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can I assume that you just were not aware of that information, as opposed to you were aware of it and simply didn't think it was necessary or helpful to look at?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: For the total number, I did not think about that as a source. I think your point is good that military deaths before 11th of July should be excluded, because we're only looking at missing persons after the 11th of July. So if it could be shown that some of these were -- actually happened before the 11th of July, they should definitely be excluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But -- and I don't know because I haven't seen the list, but if there is a list of military dead, you know, and if we are to assume that some 5.000-plus or minus or so of the 15.000 or so folks that went to Tuzla were armed, and if we are to assume that many, perhaps a lot more than 5.000 -- of the 15.000 were within the age bracket of 16 to 60, and knowing that everyone -- most of those folks were mobilised at the time, okay, don't you think that looking at the military list might have been helpful to see whether some of the folks that went missing in the woods as they were fighting by Zvornik to get to Tuzla might have been on that list?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, although I -- but I think you beat me in the number of ifs in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're absolutely correct on that. The difference is the material and documentation was available to you and not available to me, and you're the expert, I'm not. Right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It was available to my successor at the -- who is on this project.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Had you asked your successor to make it available to you in preparation for your addendum or in preparation for your testimony here today. Do you think that your successor would have been cooperative in providing you that information?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Very much so, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So it's not for lack of uncooperation, but a lack of perhaps a need on your part to look at that information?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Perhaps a lack of imagination on my side. But in my addendum I did not present any new numbers of missing persons. I just wanted to comment on the few aspects relevant for the whole situation, for analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, the reason I'm heading down this path, and the reason I'm being kind of direct with you on this is not so much because of the numerical figure that you've arrived, but it would appear, would it not, sir, that since you left the project, you have written an article called "Accounting for Genocide." Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And for the record, this will be marked as D110 for identification. We're not going to go into it right now in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But I'm sure before coming here today - and with the cautionary instructions from Mr. Waespi - you probably did read all of your articles before coming here to -- in preparation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I looked over them, but not in detail because I have been very busy dealing with other business.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, forgive me if I have looked at the details. In this particular article, you also state - and we're going to get to it - but you state that you wanted to assess the magnitude and demographic impact of the massacre, as you called it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It can be found on page 4 of your report --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Of my 2000 report or the article?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The article. I'm sorry. I'm not going to discuss it that much, other than to say that it would appear that you stated that you had two following questions. Question one: What was the magnitude of the massacre relative to the pre-war population. And question number two: From whence came the missing men to Srebrenica before the fall of the enclave. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, since we're at this topic I want to be very clear. From listening to your testimony, in reading your report, it seems that that was not part of your initial mandate from OTP. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: You could say that. This is not a legal document, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It's a scientific paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, okay. There's no need to get the -- on the defensive side yet. My question is: When you were initially hired by the Office of the Prosecution, seconded and then later became a contract employee of the United Nations, were you not initially asked to look at how many people were missing in total as a result of the war and then slowly narrowed into how many people were missing as a result of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The initial mandate was not about the number missing; it was the number -- demographic effects in general, including number of deaths and refugees and displaced persons, and then after some time I was asked to study Srebrenica, the case of Srebrenica in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And the issue was: You were to try to estimate and validate the number of missing persons from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. This is from your testimony, by the way. I just looked at it -- from the Krstic case, that is. Now, that was your mandate. Right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say that you were never asked by the Office of the Prosecution to make a determination as far as the impact, you know, these -- on the Srebrenica community?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, they would like to know, I think, how many people who lived in Srebrenica who were killed. They were very interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that's one question. And in fact --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: And at that time, when I did this, we could not tell because we hadn't -- we did not know how many people who were in the enclave before it fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And we still don't know.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We have this figure of 40.000, perhaps slightly less, slightly more. Right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- I guess we're going to have to get to this article at this point, just to pin you down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I have copies of your article. Again I'm referring to D110/1 for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe you have the -- you may want to look at mine only because it's easier for me to focus you, but I see that you have the nice published version.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Excuse me, which -- this is not the final version. I don't know where you have got this copy from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I got it from the office of -- "Accounting for Genocide: How Many Were Killed in Srebrenica." That was 10 July, 2002. It has an ERN number 01121235. And I can only assume that this was provided to us by the Office of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I do not recall. It could be that this is the version I submitted to the OTP for permission to publish and that later there were -- some changes were made later. Because I recognise in the acknowledgments, there are more names in the final version than in this version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I suspect that since we're going to go into tomorrow, you'll have the kindness to provide me with a copy of the actual one so I can give it a quick over.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Although there are probably not very large differences between these two versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I could focus your attention -- and again I'll look at your version and if you have changed, please feel free to comment on it because I certainly don't want to appear unfair. If you could look at page 4, and we can even put it on the ELMO, if there's an extra copy. I believe we do have an extra copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Usher. Sorry for troubling you. Page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You could almost tell it's a draft because you have a little notation to yourself, "include map of Bosnia", so that's how I knew it was a draft, but this is all they gave me. All right. Now, there you state on page 4, and I'm reading right before the two bullet points. You say: "The research questions that guided the demographic project on Srebrenica were defined by the Office of the Prosecutor as: What was the minimum number of victims from Srebrenica who were killed by the VRS after the fall of the enclave on 11 July, 1995, who can be identified by name?" Okay. And two: "What is the reliability of this list of victims?" Okay. Further down, if we skip one paragraph, you say: "In addition to the two research questions posed by the Office of the Prosecutor, we" -- I can only assume when you say "we," you're including your colleagues, or at the time it was a student. Henrik Urdal and Lyngstad. Okay. So you say: "We also want to assess the magnitude and demographic impact of the massacre." Okay. And: "The following questions are concerned with these matters." And that's when you state: "What was the magnitude of the massacre relative to the pre-war population? From whence came the missing men to Srebrenica before the fall of the enclave?"
