So just so I'm clear, was it your understanding and belief that at the time that you were hired by and working for the Office of the Prosecution, your mandate included just the initial first questions, or did they also include the questions that you state further down where you say you wanted to assess the magnitude of the massacre?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: They were not so clear on that, what was the magnitude relative to the pre-war population. But I think it was mentioned because I had made several attempts at getting lists or information about the population in Srebrenica immediately before the fall of the enclave. I was in touch with several international organisations who were there to, say, UNHCR, did they have a list of the number of the people there, and -- but I did not get anywhere on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, was this something that you felt was necessary to the project, or was this something that the OTP was interested in, given the fact that they wanted to see whether or not they should indict anyone for the charges of genocide, if you know?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But it would seem - and I don't want to get ahead of myself - but in reading your article it would seem that you come to some conclusion of your own, that because of the magnitude and the impact on the community, this was genocide?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's true. And the article -- the name of the article is "Accounting for Genocide". Although this was not -- wasn't meant in a legal sense but in an, you could say, academic discussion about genocides. And there's reference in the article to other genocides, whether they have been taken to court or not. And we knew, and as you also stated, you agree that a large number of people were killed. We don't know exactly how many. Some died from -- were not killed but died on the way from various causes. But a large number of men were killed, and so it is not unnatural to say that this may be a genocide. Now, as you also know, if I may, there is no precise definition of genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, rather than discuss the issue of -- the definition of genocide, getting back to what you claim to have been one of your purposes for your study and getting back to my initial question, don't you think it would have been relevant then to have made the effort to see how many were actually killed on the way to Tuzla as a result of the ongoing battles that were going on?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: For legal purposes, yes. But for -- say for general -- or general analysis, it doesn't really make much difference whether they were killed fighting or killed in other ways, because it's not always easy to distinguish between those and if there is -- well, say --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Collateral damage.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Collateral damage is one thing, and if it's part of the whole fight, say in the Second World War, when six million Jews were killed, whether some of them were not massacred but killed in action, and there were some in Warsaw that were killed in action. It doesn't really make much difference. It was an attack on the Jewish population and whether or not they were killed in action wasn't -- for posterity is not a big issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So it seems -- well, in reading your article here, it would seem that you have come to some sort of a legal conclusion of your own?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Not a legal conclusion, more a scientific conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, getting back to what information was not known, okay, what data is unavailable for your study, can you give us a list of the data that you would have liked but was unavailable to you as a result of lost records, incomplete records, mistaken recording, can you give us a list of that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Of course I would like a list of all people who died in connection with the fall of Srebrenica and the cause of death, place of death, time of death, and of course name, et cetera, date of birth of all the individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did you do an accounting of where the people were listed as their place of death, whether -- how many were listed to have been killed in Potocari, how many were listed killed in the woods? Do you have a breakdown of that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I don't recall if we have that. We did have it at some stage. I don't recall now that we -- it was -- maybe if you let me, I will have a quick look. But you seem to be more familiar with my paper than I am, so perhaps you remember whether there is a breakdown.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have to be honest, I'm not very good with your charts -- at understanding them.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, we did not focus very much on that. At some stage we did an analysis, but the place of disappearance, no, we did not focus much on that, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the data that you did rely on, we'll talk about that first. As I understand it, you had a list that came from the ICRC, the Red Cross, in essence.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I had two lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, you had two lists. But we'll talk about in a general sense the sources. The sources were the ICRC. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then you had the PDH?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: PHR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: PHR. And those were the physicians for human rights. Right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then for other reasons which we'll get into, you looked at the 1991 census?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then you also had a voting list that was composed or compiled by OSCE in 1997/1998?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And as I understand it, getting back to the two -- all of these lists, you know, were obviously created for different reasons. Okay. Right. You're shaking your head. You've got to --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not shaking; I'm nodding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. And they -- by different organisations. Right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At different time periods?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Different questions were asked or the questionnaires were different?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: And the purposes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And their purposes were different.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: -- were different, and instruments for collecting data were different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the instruments. And if we could encapsulate your entire study, as I understand it - and I'm going to do the best I can as a layperson - in essence what you did was you had a list. Once you cleaned up or compiled the ICRC list and the PHR list, you merged them; and from there, you compiled a master list. And for purposes of corroboration and to double-check, you used the 1991 census and you used the voting list. And I'm speaking in a very general, broad approach. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct. You got the major points.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So let's -- so those were the sources. Question: To your knowledge, were there other available sources? We talked about one, the military list, but let's forget that. We can deal with -- we've dealt with that. Were there other available lists that you knew of at the time, or might have learned thereafter, that have been examined?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Not that I knew about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Because of course then I would have used them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I'm a data freak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Well, good. Now, of the four sources that you used, would I be correct in stating that only one of the sources was official, in a sense that it came from a government as opposed to NGOs?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And that would have been the 1991 census?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Conducted at about the time of the war, right before the war was about to break up -- to start. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: 31st of March, 1991, was the census day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And we're going to get into it. But as I understand from reading your historical analysis of the census of 1991, because of the war and the conditions there was never an opportunity to come up with a clean list. I believe that was the word that you used or phrase, to clean it or to have a comprehensive list. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Especially as there may be -- were many errors in the data and they were not checked and corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we're going to get to that in a little bit. But aside from the sources that you checked, were you aware of whether the UN had a list of refugees and other persons that were threatened by war, that list being in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, I did not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I heard about, though, a list of displaced persons in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. There's a list of that as well.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: After the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: After the war, an OHR.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: And I made an attempt to get that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to get to that. But I just -- let me go through my list and then we're going to get to your list. Okay. Were you aware that the UN had a census of refugees -- of refugee households in the RS?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I vaguely remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: You mean the UNHCR when you talk about UN?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, yeah, UNHCR. But it was a list of refugee households in the RS. Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, I think I remember something about that, though this is now six years ago. We did -- UNHCR was not willing to provide any data on individuals to ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, might I be able to look somewhere in your report -- because I'm a footnote fetish, you know. I'm that kind of nut. I like footnotes. I like to read them; I like to go to the source. I haven't been able to find anything where you've gone and made these requests and they were -- they said, We're not going to provide them, a UN organisation to another UN organisation. Could I find that anywhere in your reports or your articles?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Probably not -- no, I don't think so. And I don't see why I should have included that, all the things that failed would be very strange to -- even you might get too many footnotes from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, I guess -- and then we're going to go on, and there's a reason for all of this, of course. Did you look at the voter list for Serbia, the 2000 one?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: For Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah. To see whether -- because -- I mean the census.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Are you talking about Bosnia or Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah -- no, for Serbia, the census, the final results.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It was not available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about the final results of the census of 2001 in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No. This was after I did this project.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. There's an official -- I'm told, and we can dig it up, that if you were to go, for instance, to the RS Bureau of Statistics, there is an official assessment of the inhabitants of the RS that goes from 1996 all the way to 2003. Did you check that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Did you have -- in another paper I did find some data on a so-called census in Republika Srpska in 1994 or 1995 or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But they have it all the way to 2003?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: This work was does in 1999 and 2000, so I was not aware of that source.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But what I'm saying to you: Were aware that they have official assessments that go all the way up to, which would include the period when you were working --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. What about -- did you ever check the results of the vital statistics of the RS? And as I understand it they have official records, if you go to Banja Luka, from 1996 all the way to 2003.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I really wanted to use the vital statistics, but in a situation where there is war and conflict, the vital statistics are very deficient. And I doubt very much that the vital statistics for Srebrenica would have helped me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But just so we know that we're all speaking on the same page, the vital statistics would have the births and the deaths and I think they also include the marriages as well.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Fair to say that aside from the four sources that you have mentioned, you didn't reach out to see what other sources might be available, if not to answer your first question - that is how many people perished as a result of the Srebrenica incident - but the second question which you seem to be interested in and that is the impact on the Srebrenica community?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You would agree with me that if you were writing a paper and you were trying to make an assessment as to the impact on the community upon which you were to conclude in your own paper that a genocide had occurred, that you might want to look at statistics from sources as the one that I've indicated. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just one point to raise. This witness has been called for purposes of cross-examination on his report, especially the additional one of 2003. And now we are going into his academic papers and -- so I'm not entirely sure whether that was the purpose why this witness has been called to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Waespi, we believe that all those cross-examinations are related to the subject matter we are discussing, about Srebrenica, which might - I do not know at this moment - have some relevance to that very issue. Up to now we didn't see that the Defence counsel has passed this boundary yet. But we will be very careful on that, thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You have to bear the objections from the Prosecution in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I surely do, Your Honour, and I'm playing within the field. I may get offside occasionally, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, did you recall -- do you remember my question, or would you like me to ask it all over again?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Maybe I can say something, maybe I'm not quite to -- on your point. But to assess the impact of the population on Srebrenica, you would need another census. And there were plans for a census in 2001 for all of Bosnia, but the international community would not let the census be taken because -- for various reasons. And since I was not aware of any census, there was no data on the complete population composition of Srebrenica in -- after the war, I mean, 2001, or after 1995. Moreover, there were large refugee movements, not only Muslims being driven away from Srebrenica, but then Serb refugees or displaced persons moving to Srebrenica, including from areas of Sarajevo that were after the Dayton Accords where then became part of the Federation and many people left. So far as I understand, many of the houses in Srebrenica are now inhabited by people from Sarajevo and probably there -- and also the other way around..

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Of course, before the war Srebrenica was a multi-ethnic community. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Actually, you have some statistics on it. Right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When Srebrenica fell, for lack of a better term and I'm not asserting a legal connotation to this, but for lack of a better term, was not Srebrenica ethnically cleansed of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It was first ethnically cleansed of -- before the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah, how many Serbs were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Before 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right before the fall of Srebrenica, 1995, July 11th, was Srebrenica not ethnically pure of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I do not know. We have the census from 1991, and I do not recall, but there was a certain, as you said, multi-ethnic society. There was no census or enumeration of people before the 1995 fall, so we don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But do you know -- well -- so as we stand here today, you're not aware whether -- when Srebrenica had been declared an enclave, when Naser Oric was in there with his army, the 28th Division, you're not aware -- and you had the various brigades of the VRS surrounding the enclave, you're telling us that you were not aware whether Srebrenica had any Serbs living there at the time?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I knew there had been -- had been fighting and atrocities from both sides, but I had not seen any population estimates of the number of Serbs or Croats or Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. We'll leave that for another day. Now, getting back to your stated purpose -- because here in your article you state in the conclusion, and I'm referring to page 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, this has been marked for identification purposes as D110.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You state -- and I'll just read and tell me if it has been changed. You'll have to accept my apology on the record for that.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Page 12 you have a conclusion. And here you say: "The aim of this article has been to present the results and the methods used by the authors to establish a minimum estimate of victims of the genocide in Srebrenica based on individual-level data." All right. Just from this sentence can we not conclude that you have made, at least in your own mind, a conclusion that a genocide occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, he was asked this question before --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask -- I haven't --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Twice, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I ask the follow-up question, perhaps Mr. Waespi will see that there's a foundational reason why I'm asking this question. Just one more question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think you have already asked this question and the witness has already answered it, and we are satisfied with the answer. If you have any follow-up questions, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just didn't want to be unfair to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when you -- since you have determined that genocide occurred, may I ask: Was that based on a numerical figure, that is, coming up with 7.456 or 57 or whatever, or was that based on your assessment and analysis and expert opinion on the impact, the overall impact, these atrocities would have had on the community?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It was based on the numerical figure, that 7.500 people who are dead. It is a very large number. And in -- except in a legal sense, I think, for historians would be satisfied to call this a genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I just have a question here. In one of the footnotes -- I don't know if it's in this one. In one of the footnotes to an article that you make reference to, I believe it's in your 1993, you make reference to -- the reference is to a paper that was prepared by Ball, Patrick, and it deals with killings and refugee flow in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I looked at it and I noticed that there was a -- that you chaired a reviewing panel for this particular paper.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Some 70 pages, it looks quite academic. Was there a reviewing panel for your article that you prepared?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No. It's unusual to have review panels. But -- no -- well, when you submit an article to a paper, there's always a review. There are the editors and the referees. And yes, my article was reviewed by referees, anonymous referees. So the draft that you presented to us dated 10th of July was presented to a journal that reviewed it and gave some comments, there were a few changes made, and it was accepted. And they wrote they were very happy to receive this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: So that is the normal procedure in the academic world. Whereas, if I may, the Patrick Ball paper was not submitted to a journal. If it had been submitted to a journal, it would have been reviewed in a similar way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Suffice it to say, the Patrick Ball journal, as I understand it, at least from when I looked at it --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Not the journal, the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The paper. Went through somewhat more scrutiny than yours.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I don't mean this in a negative sense, but it's just because of the nature of the papers?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It was a long and technical and difficult paper. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And going back to your paper, and again I'm referring to D110 for identification, on the very last page, page 13, at the very end, you state that -- at the very last paragraph: "We believe" -- "we" being the authors -- "believe that the large scale of the tragedy, comprising more than a third of all Muslim men in Srebrenica before the war, including about 50 per cent of all middle-aged men," and you give the ages 41 to 60 years of age, "meets the ICTY genocide criteria," and then you quote apparently from the Krstic judgement,' acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.' And then you state: "In the ICTY trial against General Radislav Krstic, the Court ruled in accordance with this view." Now, my question to you, sir, is: Did you go through any process to estimate the actual impact that these deaths would have had or have had on the Srebrenica community, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Previously you indicated that in order to make an assessment a census would have been required. Did you not state that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, but I -- since that was not available, I took another approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we're going to talk about your approaches. Was any effort made by you or the Office of the Prosecution to conduct a census, say in Srebrenica, to make a determination as to how many people are there, how many men, how many women, the ages, et cetera, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No. I did meet with the overall statistical agency for Bosnia and then discussed the census and possibility of holding a census. And we agreed in principle that there should be a census. It would not have been enough, though, to have a census of just Srebrenica, since there was -- have been so large movements of people in and out. So a census of the population of Srebrenica after the war would not have told us anything, because we needed to know where they came from and where those who lived there, where they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And for the purposes of your studies, since you know that would have been relevant information, could you not, sir, have come up with a questionnaire where you could have gotten that information, received that information, and then perhaps check it against other sources. You could have done that, could you not?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: My capacity was unfortunately limited. It was myself and one assistant. We did not have the capacity or the resources to conduct a partial or full census. All my work relied on data that was collected for other purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to get to that data, but I guess I'm trying to get you to think outside the box. Did you ever make that request to say, if we're going to have a study in order to demonstrate the impact on this community in light of some of the limitations that we have, we should have a census with perhaps some added information, was that request ever made to the Office of the Prosecution, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, but it was not -- if I may, it was not -- it wouldn't have been sufficient to have a census just for Srebrenica. It was all -- for all of Bosnia. And that I discussed with the leadership of the statistical agency, and I suggested it was very important to include questions on migration, where people lived before the war, the conflict, and where they lived afterwards. And the statistical agencies said the international community will not let us have a census yet; we are ready for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But since we're dealing with only Eastern Bosnia, but in actuality Srebrenica, could you not have accomplished or compiled a list similar to the list that was compiled by the ICRC, with the exception is that you would go from house to house to house to count heads, to determine their sex, to determine where they came from, whether they were residents of Srebrenica or whether they had been refugees or displaced persons that were living in somebody else's home, was that not available to you as an option? I'm not saying about the resources; we'll forget about the resources. Was that not an available option as far as looking for data, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I don't think it would have been very helpful, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So the answer is: It wasn't necessary to do that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I did not consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That's a more honest answer now. Now we're talking. That's what I'm saying, I'm trying to get you to think outside the box. So if you hadn't considered it, you could not have made that step to ask the Office of the Prosecution to see whether resources are available to do such a questionnaire analysis. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And when we're talking about Srebrenica, and I assume you've been there, we're not talking about New York City, we're not talking about Oslo, we're not talking about The Hague, we're talking about a pretty small place, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, did you -- have you -- since coming here today, have you asked to check the voter registration for the years, say -- I guess they had a vote 1997. I think they had -- there's a list -- current list available, 2003. Have you checked the list to see how many on that list actually live in Srebrenica and how many are voting from outside the country who are from Srebrenica? And Norway, as I understand, has a lot of people from Bosnia living there who vote in -- who vote, you know, absentee. Did you look at that list?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: We did look at that list for 1997/1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It's not reported here, but we did look at the number of people, as you said, who were from Srebrenica and lived elsewhere and other way around, and so on and all kinds of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, this would have been a source. Right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The answer is yes --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, not for the number of persons who died in connection with the massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No. I understand. But it is a source of information nonetheless that you looked at. Right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it it must have had some significance because you looked at it, otherwise you would have said, no, you know, I don't need this information; it's not necessary. But nonetheless you looked at it. Right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, and what did I find?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know yet.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: You are not interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to get there. What I do know is I have nothing in here in either your reports or your articles that states that you looked at this information, and here is why this particular information is irrelevant. I don't have anything in here. Right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, aside from the issue of how many people perished overall, okay, that numerical figure, would that information not have been useful if we were trying to make some sort of an estimation on people that were from Srebrenica that were abroad or who were in BiH?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. We did that, and we found that -- we looked at the ethnic cleansing of Srebrenica and found that it was totally turned around. There were very few -- there were few, if any, Muslims in Srebrenica after the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: After the conflict -- okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: After the massacre or the fall of the enclave. There were some -- many people who were from Srebrenica who registered to vote elsewhere, especially in Tuzla and Sarajevo. But from those originally there and who were Muslims, there were a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you have the numerical breakdown?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Not here, but my successor Ewa Tabeau has looked at this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between question and answer. Would the counsel please use the microphone, otherwise the interpreters cannot hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, my figures show that for the 1996/1997 list, you had 13.094 Muslims, 11.043 Serbs that were registered to vote in Srebrenica, with 4.000 Muslims registered to vote from abroad. So we're talking at about 17.000 eligible Muslim voters. Okay. Does that correspond with the figures that you looked at, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you're going to be publishing an academic article where you're stating an opinion where you're trying to conclude the ramifications of a community based on the number of deaths - and of course you do give some breakdowns based on your theory - would it not have been reasonable to then look at also what the results might be in 2003; in other words, how many people are registered to vote in Srebrenica who are actually living in Srebrenica and also how many are registered from abroad, would that not have been helpful as well?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Perhaps. I think so. With limited resources, I did not have time to do that. But I would like to draw your attention to the fact that we did look at the proportion of men who lived in Srebrenica in 1991 who were found to be dead or missing in relation to the conflict, and that a third of the men, approximately, in some age groups more than half of the men, were listed as missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: And that is indeed a significant part of the original Srebrenica population. So we did consider that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And we haven't got to that part, and I understand that you did look at that and you did make some findings. What I'm interested to know is: Aside from those lists that you've indicated, the four lists, why did you not reach out and look at other available data before reaching conclusions which you are publishing, either in reports or in journals, which you've indicated have been received with a great deal of interest in your field?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: We did look at the voters' lists, we did use it. We did not look at the ethnic cleansing aspect, if that is what you are considering. The voters were the people who are registered to vote. And we could have done that, of course. But we needed -- in an academic article, you need to focus on certain issues, and that was our focus.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that because somebody is living in Oslo, working there and voting in the RS, that he's there as a result of ethnic cleansing, is that a conclusion that you axiomatically draw? They are in Norway, hence they must be ethnically cleansed?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I did not say anything about that. You would like me to have looked at hose data. And I did not. So perhaps you should do this study.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But if you're going to be making a conclusion with respect to the impact on this particular community, today as you testify here in court, all right, do you think that would be useful information?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I think it would be useful information, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: To see, for instance, how many births, how many new people are on the voting list as a result of getting older and becoming eligible to vote. That would be important, right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, but not highly related to the number of people that were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How many men are living in Srebrenica that are Muslim. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How many children are there. Right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: But still we are focused on the number of killed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In all due respect, he questioned him at length now about what should be part of an academic or scientific article. It doesn't really go into his report because that was a different mandate given by the OTP, and the OTP certainly didn't tell him to publish anything in an academic article. So in my belief, I think that goes now beyond what the reason was he was called to be cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe Mr. Karnavas could think it over during the break. Now it is time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. I finished that area. And just for the record, I'm basing my cross on what the Prosecution has argued in the Krstic judgement -- or the Krstic trial at the end of the case. And I apologise if these are issues that they should have raised at some other point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll resume at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the record I just want to clarify a couple of things, because I misspoke when I said that the 1997 voter list had 4.000 that were abroad, that was inclusive within the 13.094 Muslims that were registered to vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And also the latest voters list, you might be interested to know, is 2.000.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: May I make a comment, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You certainly may, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: You also referred to the 1996 voters' list, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The 1996 voters' list is not relevant to use at all because it's included the 1991 census. There was no collection of voters' registrations for the 1996 elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So your -- what you're telling me now is that you actually looked at that voters' list?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, I did not consider it. I used 1997 and 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, okay. I'm trying to tell you that for my information that I'm referring to it's the 1996/1997, that's where I got these figures from. Now -- but we'll move on and we'll get back to the voters' list at some point. Initially -- I want to talk to you now about the sources that you did use, and the two primary sources initially were the list that was compiled by the ICRC and the list that was compiled by the PHR. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, with the ICRC, they have compiled, I believe since the war and thereafter, several different lists. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The ones that you had available were --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: A qualification, please. Not several different lists. They have updated, revised previous lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. And thank you for correcting me.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: They have published different lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right, exactly. And I appreciate for that correction. And you had the third and the fourth edition, I guess, if we could call it that.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So one of the first tasks that you had was to take a look at the third and the fourth to make sure that there were no duplications?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Because, as I understand it, as people were declared missing, they might have been added on; and as people who had been found who were declared missing were struck off. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And also there might have been situations, I assume, where somebody might have been listed as missing by different sources, different people, different relatives. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, can I ask you what the percentage of error was when you compared these two lists.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: What do you mean by error? Do you mean duplicates?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Duplicates.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I don't recall. Not a very large number. I would need to check the records. It's not included in my report, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't believe I see a percentage, as far as, you know, that this was within a margin of 3 to 5 per cent or anything of the sort, as far as errors go. In fact, would it surprise you that I don't have that for any of your reports where you indicate what the percentage of error was? Would that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, it would not be included not to overburden the report with details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, surely that little space wouldn't have been that much of an overburden, would it?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Then you would have to define what is meant by a percentage error.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you think that that might have been relevant, at least maybe not to put into your report, but at least to make some sort of determination about the quality of the reporting -- of the list itself?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, we included such data in basic reports. We did look at it and -- but we did not include, as I said, all details about the study in the final report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me just -- because you have to forgive me, this is not my field of expertise. When you went through the list - and I take it you went list - you first checked each list, and then you compared the lists. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, we merged them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But before merging them, did you check the list itself first to see whether they had any duplicates, any errors?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, my question is: At that point in time, did you subscribe a numerical percentage of the errors found, such as this list has 10 per cent errors of duplications, or five per cent, or two per cent?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Not per cent, but we did count the number of duplicates. It wasn't a very large number. Much, much less than 10 per cent. As far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, for statistical purposes, is there a margin of error that's an acceptable range?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: There's no objective margin of error. We're not talking about probabilities here; this is not probability theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I suspect that you kept track of the list of names, along with all the other relevant data, of all those who were duplicates or you thought to be error?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So for instance, if I were to ask the Office of the Prosecution to provide me with that analysis, that information, they might be able to accommodate me?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, when you made the comparisons, at that point is it fair to say that since you didn't do a percentage check on the first individually, that you probably didn't do a check to see what percentage of error existed when you merged the two?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Of course when you merge the two, there was a very large overlap, many duplicates, because basically the 1998 version, the fourth version, was an update of the third version. So it means that 1995 percent [sic] of the individuals were the same in both of these. So we just had to make sure that they were marked as such and not repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Some -- there were some additional names in the 1998 version, and some names were -- there was a very large overlap, but some names only in the third edition and some names only in the fourth version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then I take it, based on that, you compiled, for lack of a better term, a master list from ICRC?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, once you had that list of names, might I ask, that master list, was it composed after checking all of the data, the name, surname, name of father, date of birth, year of birth, place of birth, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And may I ask: From that master list, of which I believe it was -- how many thousands was it? 6.000 or something? 5.000?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Approximately 7.000, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 7.000, that's when you add the folks from the PHR. Right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, there is an additional number of people from PHR. It was very small, just a few hundred. So I think it's more in the order of 7.500.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what was the percentage of folks on the list, names on the list, where you had incomplete data? Did you make some kind of a breakdown --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So -- and what was the percentage of names that had incomplete data that you then needed to go to other sources or to do other things to fill in the blanks as best you could?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Let me check. On the ICRC lists, date of birth was complete for 65.4 per cent. So that is full date of birth, day, month, and year. So that means that 35 per cent did not have the full. But there were only one or two cases where there was none of that, no year of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: And date of disappearance was 89.6 per cent complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's stay with this for a moment. And these are not trick questions. This is just to -- I'm trying to understand this. We know from this report that approximately 35 per cent at least did not have a complete date of birth. Can I assume or can we assume here that all the other information, such as the father's name and then the place of birth, were completed? Or is this just representative of date of birth incomplete or complete information?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: There were errors in all variables, misspellings, and errors to a smaller or larger extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Data of completed birth is to the larger extent. But no data are perfect, ever, not even in Norway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: With that qualification, and I'll grant you that, did you do a breakdown so we can see what the percentage was from this list of missing information in each category, such as, you know, the identification number, the date of birth, the name of the father, the place, is there a numerical breakdown?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I think the OTP will be happy to provide you with that. The identification number was not included in the ICRC list, by the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you said that they would be able to provide me with that information. Does that mean that a numerical breakdown was done, or am I going to have to do it myself? I mean, with my large staff and all the resources we have, we could do that.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: OTP could easily do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. But needless to say, as you sit here today and having written these reports, this wasn't something that you or your team had compiled, this sort of data?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The ICRC list?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah, from the list. We're going to go one by one. In other words, when you checked all of this, did you say -- because as I understand you had an assistant but later on there were other students, and later on there was a demographic section within OTP, did you ever request that a breakdown be done so then we can have this information?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I remember looking at that myself and -- but we did not include all that information in the report, again not to overburden it. But we included the breakdown on complete date of birth and date of disappearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I can see that from the report, sir. And I'm not asking you whether you wanted to overburden this report, okay. And trust me, I've been burdened by it as it is, okay, Lord knows. But aside from that, is there information in the file where you looked at this and gave -- you know, gave it some significance, or perhaps you felt it wasn't necessary, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I looked at it, certainly. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you actually did the breakdown?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I think so for most of the variables, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So I can ask the OTP to provide me with a list of the breakdown, and they would be able to say for 30 per cent there was no place of birth, from 20 per cent the names didn't match --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And that's already been done. You've looked at it and felt it wasn't significant in any way?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, it was significant in the overall impression about the data quality. So I learned about the data quality and made a conclusion on the quality based on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: But, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It's not only missing data or not. It's also whether there are errors in the data themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, that was my next question.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Spelling of names, date of birth, and so forth. So those data were also evaluated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Overall can you give a numerical figure or a percentage figure of how many on the list checked out completely versus the ones that had problems, either with misspellings or omissions?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That isn't -- it's not possible to give you an objective answer because it's not -- first we would have to define what is meant by an error.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: So if you were on the list and your name had one spelling mistake, one letter wrong, two lettered twisted, interchanged, is that a serious error or is it just an error or... Such considerations would have to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's take that example. First you would have to -- you would agree with me that at least on its face it might seem like an error. Right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So the next thing would be to see whether that can be verified or rectified?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So you might then need to go to another source that might have part of that information or maybe more information. And when you dovetail it, you can come -- have a more complete picture. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So would you agree with me that if you were to find additional information that would corroborate part of it and correct other, then that would be an error, the initial name on the list, as it stood?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So see, very easily, we solved that definitional problem, we have a definition of errors. My question is: Did you and your team list or compile a percentage of errors? You know, just an overall figure to tell us how many errors were in this list, whether they were because of misspellings or maybe there was a missing number to the personal identification, or the father's name was misspelled or so on and so forth. Can you give us a figure, if you know?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: If I may, I would have to say something about the methodology on this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before you get to the methodology, could you just answer my question and then -- we're going to get into the --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The methodology is a necessary part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is the answer to my question, no, you did not compile a percentage of --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I would need to say, how do you detect errors? We detect errors by comparing the list on missing persons to other sources, as you correctly say, especially the census now. If you manage to match records on both lists that are identical, then -- exactly, then there is no error. But there are a number of records that we cannot match, perhaps because of errors, perhaps not. So some of the errors are detected, some are -- there are also unknown errors. And we kept a record of -- during this matching procedure, how many matches were done with everything, say complete name of birth, complete name, complete -- including father's name, complete date of birth, et cetera, how many matches with the census were exact. And so on. The next time we would just need to include year of birth. But you know, there are also errors in the census. So when there is a difference, whether it is due to an error in the missing list or the census list, that is not clear always. When there are two different years of birth, how do you know which one is the correct one? We did so-called fuzzy matching we looked at individuals with the same name, but perhaps we checked whether -- if we didn't find, whether they were born one or two years apart to allow for errors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Are you through with your explanation for now on this?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Are you happy with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure I'm happy, because I still have some questions, but I accept your explanation which I found in your report incidentally. But getting back to my question, because we haven't gotten to matching yet. You see, I'm still back on the first list, the ICRC list, and I'm trying to figure out whether after you merged the two lists to compile that master list, whether you have a numerical or percentage breakdown of how many errors in total, and then more specifically perhaps as far as names, spelling, things that you think I might be missing that you need to check --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I think -- but the detection of errors is a consequence of the merging. So we cannot speak about errors isolated from the merging.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But, sir --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: So that's how the errors are detected. We don't have a telephone directory where we can look up all the spellings of the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's set aside the errors. Do you have a listing of all the -- do you have a percentage of all the names that had incomplete data? So it's not necessarily a mistake but it's just incomplete. Do you have a percentage?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Incomplete names, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, no. Incomplete -- sir, I'm not talking about names, because there are several components. There's the first name; there's the last name; there's the name of the father; there is the complete date of birth, including the year; there is the place of missing; there is the place of birth, okay, there is the date of missing. So all of that, and perhaps more information. But with respect to that, do you have a percentage of the numbers, you know, on the list, the names on the list, that had missing information? It's a yes or no. If it's a no, it's not a problem, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I do not recall, but we could easily make such a list and provide it to you, if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So the answer is you don't know?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I don't recall. I think we made such a list, but I don't recall now. And it would be very easy to make it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I take it since I don't have that information from the ICRC list, I'm not going to have it for the PHR either?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It can easily be done?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand. Okay. Now -- because what I'm interested in is the raw data, before you do the merging. Okay. Now you have to do the merging because you want to see, I understand, the total list of people. Right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And one of your functions is to make sure, one, that there are no duplicates. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Two, that there is sufficient data for each particular name that would give you some certainty that that person, you know, actually exists and is missing. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Because, as you note, we're not talking about phantoms, we're talking about real, live individuals. And the question here was: Can we identify them by name and then perhaps later where they came from, where they were residents of, where they were last seen, when were they last seen. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you did the merging, did you come up with a percentage of -- a percentage where you had to -- a percentage of errors in the merging?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: What do you mean by "percentage of errors"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, you have one person that part of the name is misspelled. Now you have to look at somebody else, and now you're trying to get -- you look at another name from the other list, maybe the date of birth is not quite matching. And so you have to do what I believe you just called a fuzzy matching, where a little bit here, a little bit there, and then you come up with what you believe is a complete and accurate person's, you know, information.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: We kept logs of everything we did, about the matches, number of cases matched and unmatched, so on, at various stages. This was done by my assistants, and they kept logs. All of that information is available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now you said "assistants." So it's not that you just only you had one assistant, you had more than --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, one at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One at the time. Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: And those who worked on this are actually my co-authors of these papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Were they also students of demography or statistics?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I believe one of them was even your own student from Oslo?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct. Both of them took courses from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Incidentally, before we move on, once this was done, did you actually go over all of their research, or did you take it at face value that more or less they followed your instructions?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, I did a lot of checking and talking, looking at difficult cases, doing consistency checks --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Random checking?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That, too. Also looking at visual -- at names and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm having visions of the Florida counting of these ballots as we're having this discussion.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: But you will appreciate that more than 7.000 names is a very large number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree, sir.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: And that we have to automate the routines, use computer routines to do merging and checking and so on. But we do also -- I think it's very important to look at the data and get a feeling for the individual data.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, as I understand, some persons were not matched in the first rounds. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know what percentage actually did match on the first round?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I don't recall, but that is -- it's all in our logs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You then indicated that after that, going to the second round in order to match them, you broaden up the variables. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's where the fuzziness, if I call it that, because it's your word not mine, comes in?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You know. And that's where, for instance, you may play with the year, one year one way or the other. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in some instances, as I understand it, with respect to the names, rather than look at the complete name, you only look at the first initial and then the last name?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Of course, having spent a lot of time looking at these names, you came to conclude, perhaps early on, that many folks shared the same name?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The same first name as well as the same last name. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's why you would go to the father's name?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's usually one of the ways that one identifies themselves in this particular region. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And even there, even there, I am sure, I am certain - I am certain as we are speaking right now - that you found instances where the person would have the same first name, last name, and father's name. Right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I think there were such cases, but I don't recall any right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And what about the date of births? Were you able to, to some degree of satisfaction, find a date of birth for all those persons on the list?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Year of birth was found for everybody. Date of birth was found for almost everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you say "almost," what's the percentage?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It increased from 65 per cent to - it's listed here somewhere - 75.5 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So for approximately a quarter of the people on the list, we don't have a complete date of birth?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: We have year for all and in most cases month as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And that gives you a certain degree of confidence as a statistician and as a demographer that the people on the list -- that there are no duplicates where there are, for instance, you had the same first name, last name, or first initial, last name?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Let me remind you, if I may, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Go for it.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The purpose of doing this was to reduce the number of potential missing persons, because if we had not done this fuzzy matching, then the number would have been much larger. That was the very purpose, because we did not want to include the same person twice because there was a spelling mistake in the name. That would have been a serious error. Or because two persons with the same name and one was born in 1955, the other one in 1954, that they were included as two different persons. So we needed to check whether they were in fact the same person but with slight errors. In one of the exhibits for today, there is an example of a person, two persons who had the same first name, same last name, same year of birth, 1955, one has the father's name. In the other list, there is no father's name. These turned out to be two different people. But they are -- we had to be careful and check very carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And as I understand it, this list did not have that personal identification number that all the folks from the former Yugoslavia had?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct, but all the folks did not have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's correct, too. Only about 60 per cent, as I understand.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So -- and that was seven digits plus another six digits. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The seven digits basically composed the date of birth --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, please make a pause. It's too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The last six digits indicated some specific information, such as the sex, the region, the --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: And a check digit at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you did not have that information with those lists --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: In the missing lists, no. In the census, yes. In the voters' list, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But not in the PHR list?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's talk about the voters' -- the census list. I take it before you went to the census list you still had some dilemmas, otherwise you would not have gone to that source. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's true. So when there were two records that looked almost identical, we needed to go to the census to see if they really represented two different persons or the same person. And the census helped us in that, because if there were we could see in the census whether there were two persons with different names and almost the same year of birth, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I take it you had a chance, since you checked the census, to look at the census form that was used at the time. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And would that census form not include also the person's residence?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, because they were enumerated in so-called enumeration areas. So the locality and municipality were all there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And so if somebody had transferred from one area and I was living in another, would that census form not reflect that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, the census was taken on the 31st of March, as of that date. So if you leave there on that date, you would have been enumerated in the place where you lived on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was there other information on that form that would designate whether that person was actually born there or was just living there. In other words --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Place of birth was there. I think it was also place of previous residence in addition to education, occupation, and all those variables.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. I just asked that question, because going back earlier to the earlier session where we talked about taking the census in Srebrenica, see we didn't even have to compose an additional questionnaire, the census form already had all of that information, which would have provided you an understanding whether somebody had just moved to Srebrenica from someplace else as a refugee or displaced person or was actually from Srebrenica. Right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct. But still I would like to repeat that that would not have helped us in analysing the number of deaths.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that. But see, I was just going back to this issue, and that issue was dealing with the -- trying to figure out years later the impact on this community, which you seem to think was relevant in your report. Now, in that --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I may add that I was looking at the impact of the community as it was in 1991, not what happened after 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So when you were looking at the census of 1991, did you find that information to be complete or were there errors there as well?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Of course. You mentioned that already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: You said that -- one or two or three hours ago that the census was taken right at the dawn of the war and that there was no time to check the data and correct the data.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between question and answer and could Mr. Karnavas please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now -- but part of the data was apparently was either incomplete or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in part, from what I understand from reading your reports, that when the census was taken, perhaps because of poor penmanship, they were -- the spellings were wrong or there might have been even errors in the identification numbers?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Correct, but we checked for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that. Now -- and we already indicated that only about 60 or more percentage of the population actually had gone through the trouble to get a personal identification number; not everybody had one?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The personal identification number was established in 1981, and I do not know how it was distributed to people. So everybody got one, were assigned one in 1981, or for those who were born after 1981, at the time of birth or soon after. And I don't know the procedure as to where people are informed about their own identity number. Somebody may have lost the piece of paper they probably received or forgotten it for some reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On the 1991 census, can you tell me what the percentage of errors were on that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: If you excuse me, I don't think it's a very good question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well -- that's all right. Why don't you answer my question, bad as it is, and then in the meantime I'll try to think of a better one.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, we looked at one thing to assess the quality of the names, we counted the number of different names in the census for all of Bosnia, say a combination of first name and family name. First we found, I think, 120.000 names. But when you look at the names, you realise there were many typos. We corrected the typos, and then it dropped down to 80.000 or something. And the way we corrected the typos, I'm a little bit proud of it, if I may say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, go ahead. Don't be modest now.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: You know, in a household, most people in a household have the same family name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: So that if one name, say a simple name, Lukic, one is spelled Lukic straight, another one has a Y instead of a U, the third one as an E instead of an I and so on. There may be four or five different ways of spelling the same name within a household. Due to spelling mistakes or poor penmanship, as I said. Now, we compared those names in a household with a list of correct names and changed those incorrect names to the correct name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, what about missing identification numbers, what was the percentage on that from the census?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Was it like 30, 40 per cent or something. I also checked whether the ID numbers were correct because, as I mentioned, the last digit is a check digit and it's a function of the first 12 digits. So we can -- I learned the algorithm and checked in how many cases the digit was correct.
